strengths: The benchmark addresses a relevant evaluation gap by combining scientific-talk understanding, multiple input modalities, crosslingual outputs, and prompt variation within an aligned dataset.

Substantial human curation includes professional transcription and translation, expert-authored QA pairs, and annotations identifying answer availability by modality. These annotations could support useful diagnostic evaluations.
The evaluation covers 21 open-weight models across four model families and reveals substantial differences in transcription accuracy, context-length sensitivity, and prompt robustness.
weaknesses: The submission is explicitly unfinished: Section 5 labels the results intermediate and incomplete, Sections 5.2 and 5.3 contain only 'Work in progress,' and summarization analysis and text-only summarization results are missing. The absent modality ablations and QA breakdown leave central claims unsupported.

Evaluation validity is insufficiently established. BERTScore alone does not reliably measure factual correctness, abstention on unanswerable questions, or instruction compliance. No human calibration or dedicated compliance metrics are reported. Paper abstracts are used as summary references without a dataset-specific assessment of whether their information is recoverable from the presentations.

The multimodal comparisons do not control for information availability. Some questions are answerable only from video or only from audio, yet aggregate scores compare models receiving different evidence. Moreover, the AV label means either modality independently suffices, so this category does not establish a need for multimodal integration.

Scope and statistical support are limited: most tasks use only 21 NLP talks and 220 QA pairs; only summarization reaches 100 talks. All source content is English, with multilinguality introduced through translated text and target-language instructions. No confidence intervals, talk-level uncertainty estimates, or repeated prompt assignments support the ranking and robustness conclusions.

Important inference details are missing, including video frame sampling, input truncation, output-token limits, and short-context QA construction. Without these controls, severe long-form failures cannot be confidently attributed to reasoning or instruction following rather than model input limits or generation settings. ASR-to-LLM and OCR-to-LLM baselines would also help establish the value of integrated models.

Reproducibility and reporting require substantial correction. Appendix C omits the promised mixed-prompt lists, annotation-guideline links are blank, and inference code is deferred until acceptance. Table 6 links Qwen2.5-Omni to Phi-4 weights. Tables 2 and 7 disagree on Tower+ German COMET, although only BERTScore normalization should differ, and Table 7's Qwen2.5-Omni summarization entries appear to repeat unrelated recognition and translation scores.

The contamination argument is inadequate: selecting ACL 2023 material in 2025 does not establish that evaluated models have not encountered the papers, abstracts, or presentations. No contamination audit or no-context baseline tests this possibility.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a relevant evaluation gap by aligning scientific-talk audio, video, and text with multilingual tasks, short/full-talk contexts, and alternative instruction formulations.

Data curation involves professional transcription and translation, native-speaker supervision, and expert-authored QA pairs. Modality-availability and unanswerability labels could support useful diagnostic evaluations.
The preliminary evaluation covers 21 open-weight models across four model families and reveals substantial failures on long-form transcription and prompt reformulation.
weaknesses: The submission is materially unfinished. Section 5 explicitly labels the results intermediate and incomplete; Sections 5.2 and 5.3 contain only 'Work in progress'; summarization and open-versus-closed-model discussions are placeholders; and text-only summarization results are missing. The absent modality-integration and QA breakdown analyses are central to demonstrating the benchmark’s value.

Evaluation validity is insufficiently established. BERTScore alone does not reliably establish factual correctness, appropriate abstention, or instruction compliance, and no human validation of model rankings is reported. Using paper abstracts as reference summaries also risks rewarding information absent from the presentation, without a dataset-specific assessment of this mismatch.

The claimed multimodal and multilingual scope exceeds what is demonstrated. Evaluated source content is always English, with multilinguality primarily supplied through translated instructions and target text. Moreover, AV questions explicitly require only either modality independently; there is no designated category requiring joint audio-visual reasoning, and the missing modality ablations leave integration benefits unverified.

Coverage and statistical support are limited: the core benchmark contains only 21 NLP talks and 220 unique QA pairs, including just 17 audio-only and 25 unanswerable questions. Translation into additional languages does not add independent content. No confidence intervals or repeated prompt assignments establish whether ranking differences and prompt-robustness conclusions are stable.

Important controls are missing. ASR/OCR-to-LLM pipelines and no-context QA baselines would help distinguish multimodal understanding from transcription quality, slide-text extraction, and memorized knowledge. Without modality-conditioned QA reporting, the interpretation that text-only models have weaker crosslingual extraction is also confounded by questions whose answers require video.

Reproducibility is inadequate for interpreting the large long-context failures. Appendix D gives model links and library versions but omits explicit output limits, frame sampling, input truncation, and other consequential preprocessing settings. The ten alternative prompts are not provided despite the claim that they appear in Appendix C; annotation-guideline links are blank, and inference code is deferred until acceptance.

Reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results. Table 6 links Qwen2.5-Omni to Phi-4-Multimodal weights. Tower+ German translation scores differ between Tables 2 and 7 (83.6 versus 86.3), although those tables should differ only in BERTScore normalization. These discrepancies require an audit before the reported comparisons can be trusted.

The contamination argument is unsupported: selecting publicly available ACL 2023 presentations in 2025 does not establish their exclusion, or their associated papers’ exclusion, from evaluated models’ training data. No contamination check or context-free control supports the claimed mitigation.

strengths: MCIF addresses a relevant evaluation gap by aligning speech, video, and text across translation, recognition, question answering, and summarization, with four target languages and two context lengths.
Professional transcription and translation, expert-authored QA pairs, and explicit answerability labels provide a valuable foundation for a curated benchmark.
Evaluation of 21 open-weight models provides substantial baseline coverage. Fixed versus varied prompts expose potentially useful instruction-sensitivity failures.
weaknesses: The submission is explicitly unfinished: Section 5 labels results intermediate and incomplete; Sections 5.2 and 5.3 contain only 'Work in progress'; summarization analysis and text-only summarization results are missing. The absent modality ablations and QA breakdown directly concern the benchmark's central contribution.

Evaluation validity is insufficiently established. BERTScore alone does not reliably measure factual correctness, appropriate abstention, or instruction compliance. No human validation of metric rankings is reported, and paper abstracts are used as summary references without assessing their faithfulness to the actual presentations.

Multimodal integration is not demonstrated. The AV label explicitly means either modality independently suffices, rather than requiring combined evidence. Missing within-model modality ablations and no-context controls prevent distinguishing integration from unimodal shortcuts or prior knowledge.

Coverage is narrower than the framing suggests: source content is always English, all talks concern NLP, and most tasks use only 21 talks with 220 QA pairs. Translated targets do not establish multilingual speech understanding. No confidence intervals or repeated prompt sampling quantify ranking uncertainty.

Long-context failures are difficult to interpret without explicit input limits, truncation policies, frame sampling, and output-token budgets. Missing ASR-to-LLM and OCR/transcript baselines also limit conclusions about the value of end-to-end multimodal processing.

Reproducibility and reporting need correction. The promised varied prompts are absent from Appendix C, annotation-guideline links are blank, and inference code is deferred until acceptance. Table 6 links Qwen2.5-Omni to Phi4 weights; Table 7's Qwen2.5-Omni summarization entries repeat its short-context recognition/translation values, indicating a reporting error.

Selecting publicly available ACL 2023 material does not establish freedom from contamination for models evaluated in 2025. No contamination audit or context-free baseline supports the stated contamination-avoidance rationale.

strengths: MCIF addresses a relevant evaluation gap by combining scientific-talk audio, video, and transcripts with multilingual instructions and outputs. Alignment across modalities supports useful controlled comparisons.

The annotation effort is substantial: professional transcription and translation, expert-authored QA pairs, modality-specific answerability labels, and documented compensation and annotation procedures.

Evaluation covers 23 models across text, speech, video, and multimodal families, including Gemini 2.5 Flash. Per-language results, modality ablations, and fixed versus varied prompts provide several useful diagnostic perspectives.
The reported failures—partial transcription, incorrect output language, and task substitution—are practically relevant observations for developers of multimodal assistants.
weaknesses: Evaluation validity is insufficiently established. QA and summarization rely exclusively on BERTScore without human validation of correctness, factuality, or instruction compliance. Semantic similarity does not reliably distinguish correct answers from plausible but incorrect ones, and rescaled scores do not establish comparable difficulty across tasks or languages. The claim that summarization is the hardest task therefore needs stronger evidence. Language adherence, length compliance, and performance on the 25 unanswerable questions should be measured explicitly.

The multimodal-integration conclusions exceed what the QA design demonstrates. AV questions are explicitly answerable from either modality independently; there is no identified category requiring complementary audio and visual evidence. Aggregate comparisons also include questions unanswerable from a model's available modality. These experiments diagnose modality sensitivity but do not adequately establish joint reasoning ability. Matched answerable subsets, complementary-evidence questions, and ASR/OCR-to-LLM pipeline baselines are needed.

The prompt-robustness experiment contains substantive confounds. Table 7's German prompt 6 explicitly requests a summary in English, although the reference and intended output are German. Other variants introduce audio-specific wording for tasks that also use text or silent video, and the German fixed prompt specifies a maximum of 200 words while alternatives request approximately 200. These change the instruction rather than merely paraphrasing it. A single randomly sampled prompt per example, without repeated assignments or uncertainty estimates, further weakens robustness claims.

The independent data coverage is small and narrow: recognition, translation, and QA derive from only 21 ACL talks, with 220 unique QA pairs; only summarization expands to 100 talks. All source content is English, so the benchmark tests English-to-target crosslingual behavior rather than multilingual speech or video understanding. Translations do not increase independent content diversity. No confidence intervals or talk-level significance analyses establish ranking stability.

Summarization references are paper abstracts rather than summaries verified against the presented content. Abstracts can contain information omitted from a talk or emphasize different material, especially relative to an individual modality. Without a reference-support audit or human evaluation, low scores cannot cleanly be attributed to model summarization failures. The annotation process also lacks reported agreement or a quantified quality audit.

The contamination argument is inadequate. Selecting publicly available ACL 2023 presentations does not establish that they, their papers, or their abstracts were absent from the training data of the evaluated 2025-era models. Public abstracts are both references and potential memorization targets. No context-free baseline or contamination analysis tests reliance on prior knowledge.

Important implementation details and reported results need reconciliation. Frame sampling, visual resolution, audio truncation/chunking, short-context QA selection, and the BERTScore encoder are insufficiently specified. Table 8 links Qwen2.5-Omni to Phi-4 weights. Section 5.2 names MCIFfix while Figure 2 names MCIFmix. Table 2's fixed-prompt Phi4-Multimodal summarization score is 4.5, whereas Table 9's four language scores average approximately 12.9. Such discrepancies reduce confidence in reproducibility and the analysis.

strengths: MCIF addresses a useful evaluation gap by aligning scientific talks, transcripts, multilingual outputs, and several tasks across text, speech, and video. Its parallel design supports controlled comparisons between input modalities.

The dataset involves substantial human effort: professional transcription and translation review, expert-authored questions, and annotations of answer locations and modality requirements. Including unanswerable questions is valuable.

The evaluation covers 23 models and includes per-language results, modality ablations, and prompt variants. The documented annotation procedures, prompts, model versions, and planned release of outputs provide useful foundations for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central evaluation metrics are insufficiently validated. QA and summarization rely exclusively on BERTScore, without human evaluation, correctness calibration, or a human baseline. Semantic similarity does not establish factual correctness, successful abstention, or instruction compliance. Moreover, a negative rescaled BERTScore does not establish performance worse than a task-specific random baseline. Comparing QA and summarization scores also does not justify declaring summarization the hardest task.

Summarization references are paper abstracts rather than summaries independently written and validated against the presentations. Abstracts can contain information omitted from a talk and emphasize different content. Consequently, low similarity may reflect reference mismatch rather than poor summarization; the paper does not quantify this mismatch or evaluate factual coverage and faithfulness.

The prompt-robustness experiment contains substantive confounds. Table 7's German prompt 6 explicitly requests a summary in English, although the expected output is German. Other variants introduce audio-specific wording into a benchmark that also evaluates text and video, and the German fixed prompt requests at most 200 words while alternatives request approximately 200. These are changes in task requirements, not merely paraphrases, and can produce apparent instruction-following failures.

The evidence for multimodal integration limitations is incomplete. The AV question category explicitly contains questions answerable from either modality alone; there is no designated category requiring complementary evidence from both. Thus, these questions cannot directly test necessary cross-modal integration. The detailed analyses also omit Gemini, despite its leading overall performance, and lack practical ASR/OCR-to-LLM pipeline baselines.

The scope is much narrower than the broad framing suggests. Recognition, translation, and QA principally use 21 NLP presentations, with only 220 unique QA pairs; translated versions do not add independent content. All evaluated source content is English, with multilinguality primarily in prompts and outputs. The four-language setup therefore does not establish multilingual speech understanding or general crosslingual capability. Confidence intervals, talk-level uncertainty estimates, and repeated prompt sampling are absent.

Important experimental details remain unclear, including video frame sampling, model-specific input truncation, the precise construction of short-form QA contexts, and the BERTScore encoder and configuration. These details matter when attributing large long-context failures to model capabilities. Reporting default generation settings and a common output-token limit is insufficient to rule out preprocessing or inference artifacts.

The contamination argument is unsupported: selecting ACL 2023 presentations does not establish that their papers, abstracts, or related content were absent from the training data of models evaluated in 2025. No contamination audit or no-context QA baseline is provided. Together with the evaluation issues above, this leaves the benchmark's main conclusions insufficiently supported for acceptance at a selective conference.

strengths: MCIF addresses a useful evaluation gap by combining speech, video, and text with crosslingual tasks and aligned short/full-talk inputs. The parallel design supports controlled comparisons across modalities.
The dataset involves substantial human curation: professionally corrected transcripts and translations, expert-authored QA pairs, and annotations of answer availability by modality.
Evaluation covers 23 models across four model families, with per-language results, modality ablations, and prompt variants. The observed failures provide useful directions for model development.
The appendices document annotation procedures, compensation, prompts, model versions, and generation settings; the planned release of data, code, and outputs would be valuable.
weaknesses: The central QA and summarization evaluations rely exclusively on BERTScore, without validation against human judgments of correctness, factuality, or instruction compliance. Paper abstracts are used as summary references without a dataset-specific check that their claims are supported by the presentations. Consequently, low similarity does not establish summarization failure, and scores across different tasks do not establish that summarization is the hardest task.

The multimodal-integration conclusions exceed what the benchmark establishes. AV questions explicitly require information available independently in either modality, rather than complementary evidence requiring both. Moreover, Gemini 2.5 Flash, the strongest evaluated model, is omitted from the modality ablations and the purported best-model QA breakdown without explanation.

Prompt variants introduce confounds beyond paraphrasing. German summarization prompt 6 in Table 7 explicitly requests an English summary, contrary to the German reference and intended target language. Other variants specifically mention audio even for text/video conditions. Most QA and summarization prompts also leave the desired output language implicit, weakening claims that English responses necessarily violate instructions.

The effective sample size is small: most tasks use only 21 talks and QA contains 220 unique questions, including just 17 audio-only questions. Translation into four languages does not create independent content. There are no confidence intervals, talk-level significance analyses, or repeated prompt assignments to substantiate model rankings and robustness conclusions.

Long-context failures are insufficiently separated from inference limitations. Appendix D does not specify model-specific audio truncation/chunking, video frame sampling, or how timestamped answers are mapped to short clips. These details are essential to determine whether models received the relevant evidence and whether degradation reflects reasoning, preprocessing, or supported input limits.

Reported results contain material inconsistencies. Ola's long-form MCIFmix recognition WER is 6.6 in Table 2 but 36.8 in Table 10. Phi4-Multimodal's MCIFfix summarization aggregate is 4.5 in Table 2, whereas its four language scores in Table 9 average approximately 12.9. Such discrepancies undermine confidence in comparisons and require reconciliation.

Scope and contamination claims need qualification. Evaluated source content is exclusively English NLP presentations, with multilingual prompts and targets; this does not establish multilingual speech/video understanding. Selecting publicly available ACL 2023 material does not rule out contamination in models released in 2025, particularly when published abstracts serve as references. No contamination audit or context-free baseline is provided.
